title: Foundation
one_line_goal: Tools confirmed, empty project builds, riskiest ideas tested
summary: Confirm the installed tools, set up an empty Rust project with automatic checks, and test the four riskiest technical assumptions with throwaway experiments before the real app is designed. It starts only when you explicitly say go after signing off P0.

tasks.title: Confirm and record the toolchain
tasks.what: Confirms the installed tools (Rust, C++ build tools, Node, PowerShell 7), records their versions and adds the licence checker.
tasks.why: Every later result must name the exact tools it was built with.
tasks.how: Save each tool's version to a file, install only what is missing (you click the Windows prompts) and build a tiny Rust project to prove linking works.
tasks.chain: Rust 1.99, the C++ build tools, Node 24 and PowerShell 7 are already installed → confirm each works, record exact versions, add the licence checker → every later result names the tools it was built with.
tasks.check: Each tool prints its version; a tiny Rust test project builds and links; versions saved.

tasks.title: Record this computer's hardware
tasks.what: A record of this computer: CPU, memory, graphics, power plan, Windows build, and browser and web view versions.
tasks.why: Benchmark numbers depend on the machine, so results must be comparable and repeatable.
tasks.how: Run the PowerShell inventory commands listed on the phase page and save their output; you answer the CPU, memory and power-meter questions.
tasks.chain: Benchmark numbers depend on the machine → record CPU, memory, graphics, power plan and browser versions → results can be compared and repeated.
tasks.check: The inventory file holds every listed item; the web view version is re-read and compared with the one from 8 Oct.

tasks.title: Set ignore rules and licences
tasks.what: Ignore rules for build output and local data, line-ending rules, and the MIT and Apache licence files.
tasks.why: Build output and local data must not reach git, and the repo must be legally clear.
tasks.how: Write the ignore and attribute files, copy both licences from their official texts, add a licence section to the README and commit locally.
tasks.chain: Build output and local data must not reach git → ignore rules plus MIT and Apache licence files → a clean, legally clear repo.
tasks.check: Each build folder is ignored and plan snapshots are not; both licence files exist.

tasks.title: Create the empty Rust workspace
tasks.what: The empty Rust workspace: placeholder libraries in the planned folders and a pinned Rust version.
tasks.why: Every later code task needs a home with a fixed layout.
tasks.how: Create the workspace and its empty libraries in the agreed layout, keep the experiments outside it, then run build, tests, formatting and warning checks.
tasks.chain: Code needs a home → empty Rust libraries in the planned folders, with a pinned Rust version → every later task has a place to go.
tasks.check: Build, tests, formatting and code-warning checks all pass with no warnings.

tasks.title: Pin the Tauri and web-tool versions
tasks.what: Exact versions for Tauri's command-line tool, Vite and TypeScript.
tasks.why: Generated templates change under us; exact versions let the experiments be rerun identically.
tasks.how: Use Tauri's npm package, write the experiment apps by hand instead of from a template, and re-check the versions online when the task starts.
tasks.chain: Generated templates change under us → pin Tauri's command-line tool, Vite and TypeScript exactly, and write the experiments by hand → experiments can be rerun identically.
tasks.check: Experiment 1's package file has exact versions; Tauri's version is saved; versions re-checked online first.

tasks.title: Experiment 1: several web views in one window
tasks.what: A throwaway app with one window and three tab views, to test Tauri's experimental multi-view feature.
tasks.why: If the feature is unstable, the design changes before P2, not after.
tasks.how: Create the views from a background command, switch tabs by hiding and showing, and record pass or fail for resize, focus, overlap, blank pages, freezes, shortcuts and helper processes.
tasks.chain: Tauri's multi-view feature is experimental → build a throwaway app with three tab views and test resize, focus, overlap, blank pages and freezes → if it is unstable, the design changes before P2, not after.
tasks.check: Report has a pass/fail row per check, including which helper processes belong to the app; the experiment builds.

tasks.title: Experiment 2: a separate profile per site
tasks.what: A test of four ways to give each site its own browser profile.
tasks.why: Per-site isolation needs a profile chosen when a view is created, and Tauri does not offer that directly.
tasks.how: Try the routes, at least two for real; for each, check that site A's cookie is absent in site B and note the cost of keeping the route working.
tasks.chain: Per-site isolation needs a profile chosen when a view is created, and Tauri does not offer that → try four routes → pick one that keeps cookies apart, before tabs are built.
tasks.check: A route-by-criterion table; site A's cookie is absent in site B; at least two routes actually run.

tasks.title: Experiment 3: low-level WebView2 calls
tasks.what: A test of low-level WebView2 calls: suspend and resume, memory limits, crash and network events, process lists.
tasks.why: These calls sit below Tauri, and we need to know which lifecycle and security features are possible.
tasks.how: Reach each call through Tauri's escape hatch, log each result, make sure only one version of each Windows library is used, and draft safety rules per call.
tasks.chain: Suspend, memory limits and crash events are only reachable below Tauri → call each one through Tauri's escape hatch → we know which lifecycle and security features are possible.
tasks.check: Each call's result is logged; only one version of each Windows library; safety rules drafted for each call.

tasks.title: Experiment 4: test robot drives the app
tasks.what: A test of whether the Playwright test robot can drive the experiment app, Chrome and Edge the same way.
tasks.why: One fair benchmark harness must work for all of them.
tasks.how: Start each one, not as admin, with a debugging port; connect the same script, list every view, read paint timing on a local page and list what fails.
tasks.chain: Benchmarks drive browsers with Playwright through a debugging channel → connect to the experiment app, Chrome and Edge the same way → one fair harness for all.
tasks.check: The script exits cleanly, lists every view, reads paint timing on a local page, and lists what did not work.

tasks.title: Decide the design from the experiments
tasks.what: Updated risks and proposed decisions on profiles, back and forward, and the benchmark path.
tasks.why: The experiment results fix the first milestone's design before any P2 code starts.
tasks.how: Write the four results into the risk and part pages and propose new decision pages; you decide in Claude Code, then the P2 and P3 pages are revised.
tasks.chain: Four experiment verdicts → update the risks and propose decisions on profiles, back/forward and the benchmark path → you decide, then P2 and P3 are revised to match.
tasks.check: New decision pages proposed; each tested risk cites its report; you approved them in Claude Code.

tasks.title: Re-confirm the history-based wiki checks
tasks.what: A re-run of the wiki checks that use git history: raw files unchanged, page dates not stale.
tasks.why: Tampering with raw files or stale dates must still be caught; these checks were already built in P0.
tasks.how: Re-run the existing wiki check on the P1 history and its tests on sample repos; adjust the rules only if needed. No second checker is written.
tasks.chain: These checks were already built during P0 → P1 re-runs them on the new history and adjusts them only if needed → tampering with raw files or stale dates are still caught; P1 has one less real build task.
tasks.check: Sample repos trigger both rules; the real wiki has zero errors; raw-file fingerprints all match.

tasks.title: Turn on automatic checks on GitHub
tasks.what: One automatic GitHub check workflow and one local script that runs the same steps.
tasks.why: Mistakes are cheaper when caught at once, and every change is tested the same way.
tasks.how: Write the workflow for a Windows build machine and the matching local script. Claude runs the script; you push and report the GitHub result.
tasks.chain: Mistakes are cheaper caught at once → one GitHub workflow and one local script running the same checks → every change is tested the same way.
tasks.check: The local script passes; after you push, you report the GitHub result (Claude never pushes).

tasks.title: Check dependency licences and alerts
tasks.what: A licence allowlist and a known-security-problem check for third-party code, with lock files committed.
tasks.why: We must only use code we may use and that has no known holes.
tasks.how: Set up the dependency checker with licences that fit MIT or Apache, run it, and save a plan-app audit with each finding explained.
tasks.chain: Third-party code can carry unsuitable licences or known holes → a licence allowlist and a security-alert check, lock files committed → we only use what we may and should.
tasks.check: The licence and alert check passes; the plan-app audit is saved with each finding explained.

tasks.title: Start the public docs
tasks.what: Starter files for security, benchmarking and reproducibility notes, a docs index and an updated AI-use note.
tasks.why: Readers need these notes, and the docs should grow with the code.
tasks.how: Write short outlines that link to their wiki pages, then run the wiki check for broken links.
tasks.chain: Readers need security, benchmark and reproducibility notes → short starter files linking to the wiki → documentation grows with the code.
tasks.check: Files exist and link to their wiki pages; no broken links.

tasks.title: Start the literature review
tasks.what: The method for the literature review and the first batch of reading notes.
tasks.why: A research claim needs prior work, and no novelty is claimed without evidence.
tasks.how: Write the questions, sources, search terms and rules, then read the gaps the seed list names, using dated and checked sources only.
tasks.chain: A research claim needs prior work → write the search method and read the first batch, with checked sources → no novelty is claimed without evidence.
tasks.check: Method and reading-log pages exist; at least one new dated note; no unchecked citation.

tasks.title: Warn when code changes without its page
tasks.what: A check before each commit that warns when code changes without its wiki page.
tasks.why: Code and its page must change together, so the plan never drifts from the code.
tasks.how: A git hook runs the quick wiki check before each commit. Whether a hook can do this is not checked yet; it is tried in a temporary copy first.
tasks.chain: Code and its wiki page must change together → a check that runs before each commit warns when they don't → the plan never drifts from the code.
tasks.check: In a test copy, a code-only commit warns and a code-plus-page commit passes.

tasks.title: Run the gate; your review
tasks.what: One run of every P1 check on a single commit, with the output saved, then your review.
tasks.why: You see the experiment evidence and confirm or change the design before any real app code.
tasks.how: Run all automated checks, save each output, run the wiki check and mark the phase for review; you approve the exit in Claude Code.
tasks.chain: All tasks done → run every check on one commit and save the output → you review the experiment evidence and approve the exit.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist; you approved the P1 exit.

test_gate.explanation: Tools confirmed → the empty project builds and passes every automatic check → each risky assumption has a written verdict → you review the evidence and settle the design → only then does P2 start.

rows.proves: Rust code is consistently formatted, with no code warnings.
Dependencies are allowed and have no open alerts.
Plan-app style, types, tests and build pass.
The same checks GitHub will run pass here.
Playwright can drive the experiment app.
You tried Alt+Tab focus and resizing, chose the profile route, and pushed or deferred GitHub checks.
